prompt: Your RAG system returns irrelevant chunks for long queries — how do you debug it?
answer_markdown: Separate retrieval from generation before changing anything, because the two failure modes look identical from the outside. Take a failing query, run retrieval alone, and check whether the correct chunk appears anywhere in the top 20. If it does not, the problem is retrieval; if it appears but ranks low, the problem is ranking; if it ranks first and the answer is still wrong, the problem is the generation prompt. For long queries specifically, the usual cause is that a multi-part question produces one embedding that averages several topics and lands in an empty region of the vector space belonging to none of them — the fix is query decomposition, splitting the question into sub-questions, retrieving for each, and merging the results. If the query contains exact identifiers like error codes or SKUs, add hybrid search with BM25, since embeddings generalise away precisely the rare tokens you need matched. If the right chunks are retrieved but rank below topically-similar noise, add a reranker, which is usually the single largest quality improvement available to a naive RAG pipeline.

prompt: Why not fine-tune a model on your documents instead of building a RAG pipeline?
answer_markdown: Fine-tuning teaches style, tone, and output format effectively, but it is unreliable for factual recall — the model absorbs statistical patterns rather than storing retrievable facts, so it still produces confident wrong answers about specific details. Operationally it is worse in three ways: every document change requires retraining rather than a re-index, there is no way to cite which source an answer came from, and you cannot tell whether a given claim came from your documents or from general pretraining. RAG updates instantly when documents change, supports citation and therefore verification, and lets you enforce access control at retrieval time so different users see different documents — something a fine-tuned model fundamentally cannot do because the knowledge is baked into shared weights. The honest synthesis is that they solve different problems, and the common case is RAG for facts with prompting for format.

prompt: How do you choose a chunk size, and what goes wrong at each extreme?
answer_markdown: Choose it empirically against a labelled set of queries with known correct chunks, starting somewhere around 200 to 500 tokens with 10 to 20 percent overlap, then measure recall at k as you vary it. Chunks that are too small lack the context to be meaningful on their own — a sentence reading 'This applies only to orders over fifty dollars' is useless without knowing what 'this' refers to — and they fragment answers across multiple chunks so no single retrieval returns a complete one. Chunks that are too large blur several topics into one averaged embedding, which makes the vector a vague point that matches many queries weakly and none strongly, and they waste context window on irrelevant surrounding text. Two refinements matter more than the number itself: split on document structure like headings and paragraphs rather than a fixed character count, so chunks do not end mid-sentence, and prepend the document title and section heading to each chunk before embedding so it carries its own context.

prompt: A user searches for error code 'E4021' and your semantic search returns general articles about errors but not the page documenting that code. Why, and what do you do?
answer_markdown: Embeddings are built to capture meaning and generalise across phrasing, which is exactly wrong for rare exact tokens. A code like E4021 appears infrequently in training data and carries little semantic signal, so its embedding sits near the general concept of 'error codes' rather than in a distinctive location, and chunks about errors generally score higher than the one chunk containing the literal string. The fix is hybrid search: run keyword search such as BM25 alongside vector search and fuse the two ranked lists, typically with reciprocal rank fusion, which combines by rank position so it works even though cosine similarity and BM25 scores are not on comparable scales. Keyword search excels at exactly what embeddings are worst at — rare literal tokens, identifiers, names, SKUs — so the two methods are complementary rather than redundant, which is why hybrid search is close to a default for any corpus containing identifiers.

prompt: What is a reranker and why is it usually the highest-value addition to a basic RAG pipeline?
answer_markdown: A reranker is a second-stage model, typically a cross-encoder, that reads the query and a candidate chunk together and scores how relevant that chunk actually is to that specific question. The first stage — embedding search — encodes each chunk into a single vector independently of any query, which is fast enough to scan millions of documents but lossy, compressing a whole paragraph into one point and therefore surfacing chunks that are topically related rather than genuinely relevant. The reranker is far more accurate because it sees both texts jointly, but far too slow to run over an entire corpus. The pattern that exploits both is to retrieve 20 to 50 candidates cheaply by vector search, rerank those to the best 3 to 8, and send only those to the model. It is the highest-value addition because it directly fixes the most common naive-RAG failure — the right chunk was retrieved but buried beneath plausible-looking noise — without touching your chunking, embeddings, or index.

prompt: How do you stop a RAG system from confidently answering when no relevant document exists?
answer_markdown: Recognise first that top-k retrieval always returns k chunks no matter how irrelevant they are — there is no natural notion of 'nothing found' in a nearest-neighbour search, so the model receives plausible-looking context for questions your corpus cannot answer and dutifully answers from it. Add a minimum similarity threshold and return no context at all when nothing clears it, calibrating the threshold on queries you know are out of scope rather than picking a round number. Instruct the model explicitly to answer only from the provided context and to say it does not know when the context is insufficient, and make sure a few-shot example demonstrates that refusal so it has a template. Then verify grounding on the output side by checking that claims in the answer are supported by the retrieved text, and fall back to a refusal when they are not. A reranker helps here too, since its absolute scores are a better relevance signal than raw cosine similarity.

prompt: Name the four chunking strategies and explain the trade-off that no chunk size can escape.
answer_markdown: Fixed-size splits every N tokens: trivial to implement, blind to the document, and it will cut a sentence, a table row, or a definition in half. Recursive splitting is the sensible default — it tries a priority list of separators, paragraph breaks then sentence breaks then words, descending to a cruder boundary only when a chunk is still too big. Structure-aware splitting uses the document's own shape, cutting on Markdown headings, HTML sections, or code-block boundaries and never inside one, which beats everything else for technical documentation because the author already decided where an idea ends. Semantic chunking embeds each sentence and cuts where consecutive sentences stop being similar, costing an embedding call per sentence and earning that mainly on unstructured prose with no headings. The inescapable trade-off underneath all four is that a small chunk retrieves precisely — its embedding represents one idea, so it matches one kind of question sharply — but may lack the context needed to be understood or hold only half the answer, while a large chunk carries its context but averages several topics into a vague point that matches many queries weakly and none strongly. One chunk size cannot give you both; the escape hatch is to retrieve small chunks and expand to their surrounding text before generation.

prompt: Why is metadata filtering a correctness requirement in RAG rather than just a performance optimisation?
answer_markdown: Because the thing that makes embeddings useful is exactly what makes them unable to distinguish the documents you must distinguish. Last year's refund policy and this year's are near-identical in meaning, so they sit almost on top of each other in vector space; so do the same policy's copies for two different tenants. In a concrete measurement, a stale 2021 policy can outrank the current 2026 one by three parts in a million while another tenant's copy scores in the same band — gaps that are pure noise. No similarity threshold can separate those, so there is no purely semantic fix: only a predicate on source, date, language, or tenant can, which is why 'filter, then rank' is a rule rather than a tuning choice. It also has to run before or inside the vector search, never after. Filtering afterwards whittles your top 50 down to a few survivors drawn from the wrong 50, because the index never looked at the chunks the user was actually entitled to. The practical consequence is that you must store metadata at index time alongside the vector and text — retrofitting it later means re-indexing the corpus.
